newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: "Peace at last" for Australian euthanasia woman.
newsitem.headline: "Peace at last" for Australian euthanasia woman.

text.p: A terminally-ill woman has become the second person to die under Australia's world-first euthanasia law, using a laptop computer to deliver a fatal dose of drugs and bring her "peace at last".
Euthanasia campaigners said on Monday that 52-year-old Janet Mills, who was suffering from a rare form of skin cancer which causes the skin to disintegrate, committed suicide on Thursday.

"Her last words were 'peace at last' as she used a computer-driven device to self-administer a lethal dose of drugs," the National Coalition for Voluntary Euthanasia said in a statement on its "Deliverance" Internet site.
The euthanasia law came into operation in the outback Northern Territory in July. In September, 66-year-old cancer patient Bob Dent became the first to use it to die.
But an alliance of church and civic leaders are leading a legal and parliamentary battle to quash the Territory's Rights of the Terminally Ill Act.
"Quite clearly we are a nation that has come to the end of its resources," said Boak Jobbins, the Anglican dean of Sydney, after news of Mills' death.
"We no longer have anything to offer the terminally ill, the aged or the disabled but a quick exit at the end of a needle."
A backbench bill to overturn the act passed the lower house of parliament last month and is expected to go next month to the upper house Senate, where it faces greater opposition.

The controversy around the law meant that it took weeks for Mills to find a local cancer specialist to support her after travelling to the Northern Territory from South Australia. In the end she only found one after "begging" for help at an emotional news conference last month.

Mills said she had spent three years battling the disease mycosis fungoides, the rare skin cancer whose best-known victim was British comic actor Paul Eddington, star of the BBC's "Yes, Minister" series. She was frail and thin with lesions covering her face and appeared unable to stop scratching herself.
She died beside her husband and son with euthanasia campaigner Dr Philip Nitschke supervising. Nitschke, who also helped Dent die, refused to comment on her case on Monday.

"I hope that anyone else wishing to use this Act does not have to go through such a long battle to find a doctor to help them. The whole thing was very hard on me and my family," Mills said in an open letter written the day before her death.
She added: "I believe that euthanasia is the greatest thing for people who are sick with no chance of getting better. It's a wonderful idea and it stops people from suffering when they don't need to.

"I hope this law survives and is able to help others like me, who have found the suffering has become too great. It should not be overturned by the politicians in Canberra but given a chance to be made to work in the way it was intended."

Kevin Andrews, the government backbencher sponsoring the anti-euthanasia law, said Mills' death might serve as a reality check for parliamentarians soon to vote on his bill. He said the fact that Mills was from South Australia made it clear that the euthanasia law applied throughout the country and not just the Northern Territory.
But Victoria state premier Jeff Kennett, a leading euthanasia proponent, said Mills had met a "beautiful" end.

"For people in those circumstances, that form of exit is beautiful and I trust that no federal government will ever meddle with the rights of people in such circumstances to make that choice," Kennett said.
